newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria welcomes new chancellor but Klima silent.
newsitem.headline: Austria welcomes new chancellor but Klima silent.

text.p: Austria's chancellor-designate Viktor Klima broke his silence on Monday for the first time since the resignation of chancellor Franz Vranitzky but left the nation in the dark on his plans for the future.

Klima, who has shunned the media spotlight since outgoing chancellor Franz Vranitzky resigned on Saturday after nearly 11 years in power, declined to make any comment on his promotion as Austria's eighth chancellor since 1945 and leader of the dominant Social Democratic Party.
"I will only speak once I am officially chancellor," Klima told Austrian news agency APA after playing a weekend game of hide-and-seek with the press.
Klima, 49, who Vranitzky said had been reluctant to succeed him, told APA he was only entitled to make any comment on his current duties. He is still technically finance minister.
President Thomas Klestil asked Vranitzky to stay on as acting chancellor until Klima had been officially sworn in, probably some time later this week.
But Klima's silence has surprised the Austrian and foreign media, who expected him at least to acknowledge publicly what many politicians would regard as the highest honour.
Vranitzky said he had to persuade Klima to take over.

"He said he had no intention to take this job, but I convinced him my plans were better in the medium to long term," Vranitzky said on Saturday after catching the nation off-guard by announcing he was stepping down.
Austrian markets started stronger on Monday on Klima's appointment but analysts said the vacancy at the treasury may prove more difficult to fill.

"Admittedly, one does not normally associate resignations with stability but there is no doubt that this particular change will contribute to stability in Austria," said Roland Neuwirth, an analyst with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Vienna.

The timing of Vranitzky's departure was impeccable, Neuwirth said. Klima had inherited a Social Democratic Party strengthened within the two-party coalition after it won a privatisation battle over Creditanstalt bank a week ago.
Investors and analysts credited Klima with negotiating a tough two-year budget with the conservative People's Party and laying the groundwork for Austrian participation in a single European currency.
"At least we'll be getting a chancellor who knows something about the economy," a Vienna share trader said.
But a questionmark hung over who would take on the key job of finance minister and attempt to guide Austria into European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

The Austrian press were also upbeat about the new chancellor but warned the golden boy of politics had a hard job ahead to solve the key issues of neutrality and the rise of the far right led by populist Joerg Haider.
"The new strong man of Austria -- especially in these times of weakened coalition -- will have to give a sign very soon of his strength of character," respected Der Standard daily said.

Reaction over the balance sheet at the end of the Vranitzky era was mixed. Der Standard said Vranitzky's rule was inextricably linked to the rapid rise of Haider's Freedom Party, which came within 60,000 votes of the Social Democrats in last October's European elections.
Vranitzky said his party had underestimated the far right, and if he had his time again he would have handled Haider differently.
